definition: Distributional semantics is a research area that develops and studies theories and methods for quantifying and categorizing semantic similarities between linguistic items based on their distributional properties in large samples of language data.
details: The basic idea of distributional semantics can be summed up in the distributional hypothesis: linguistic items with similar distributions have similar meanings.

explainer.lead: Distributional semantics estimates how similar linguistic items are in meaning by examining how they appear across large samples of language. Its guiding idea is that items used in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings.

tiers.eli5: Imagine trying to understand new words by noticing the company they keep. If two words often appear beside the same other words, you might guess they mean similar things, just as two kids who join the same games and sit with the same friends might have similar interests.
tiers.practitioner: Apply it by collecting distributional properties for linguistic items from a large language sample, then comparing those properties to quantify similarity or support categorization. The main pitfall is treating distributional closeness as proof of identical meaning: the hypothesis supports an inference, not a guarantee, and results depend on the language sample used.
tiers.paperLevel: For linguistic items x and y, let D(x) and D(y) denote their distributional properties in a large sample of language data. The distributional hypothesis states that similar D(x) and D(y) imply similar meanings; methods in distributional semantics use this relationship to quantify semantic similarity and categorize items, although distributional similarity does not establish semantic identity.

explainer.example: Suppose “tea” and “coffee” frequently appear in similar contexts, such as near “cup” and “drink,” throughout a large text sample. Their similar distributions support the inference that the two words have similar meanings.

usedIn.name: Semantic similarity analysis
usedIn.detail: Quantifies how similar linguistic items are by comparing their distributions in language data.

usedIn.name: Linguistic-item categorization
usedIn.detail: Uses distributional patterns to group items whose usage suggests related meanings.

explainer.intuition: You can learn something about a word or other linguistic item from the contexts in which it appears. Items that repeatedly share contexts are candidates for having similar meanings.
howItWorks: Collect a large sample of language data.
Record the distributional properties of each linguistic item in that sample.
Compare the distributions of different items.
Use distributional similarity to quantify semantic similarity or support categorization.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a way to study meaning through observable language use rather than relying only on hand-written descriptions. The same distributional evidence can support both similarity measurements and categorization.
misconceptions: Similar distributions suggest similar meanings; they do not prove that two items mean exactly the same thing.
Distributional semantics compares patterns across a language sample, rather than judging meaning from a single shared context.
